summary.overview: Chapter 9 connects several core distributed-systems ideas: linearizability, causality, ordering, total order broadcast, distributed atomic commit, consensus, and coordination services. Linearizability makes replicated data appear like one atomic copy and provides a real-time recency guarantee, but it differs from transaction serializability and carries latency/availability costs. Causality is weaker: it imposes only a partial order and allows concurrent branches. Lamport timestamps provide a compact total order consistent with causality, but a timestamp order alone is not enough for online uniqueness because a node must also know the order is final. Total order broadcast gives reliable, identically ordered delivery and is closely equivalent to consensus and linearizable compare-and-set/increment-and-get. The chapter then explains distributed atomic commit through 2PC, including prepare promises, coordinator logging, in-doubt transactions, blocking, XA, and lock retention. Fault-tolerant consensus is defined by agreement, integrity, validity, and termination. Protocols such as VSR, Paxos, Raft, and Zab use epochs and overlapping quorums to provide ordered agreement as long as a majority can communicate. ZooKeeper and etcd package these guarantees into reusable coordination services.

eventual_consistency.definition: If writes stop and faults are repaired, replicas eventually converge.
eventual_consistency.weakness: It gives no bound on when convergence occurs or what a read sees before convergence.

linearizability.definition: System behaves as if one copy of each object exists and each operation takes effect atomically at one instant between invocation and response.
linearizability.rule: After a completed write, a later read must see that value or a newer one.
linearizability.concurrent_rule: A read overlapping a write may return old or new; once a new value is observed, later reads cannot revert.

linearizability_vs_serializability.serializability: Isolation property over multi-object transactions; equivalent to some serial order that need not match real-time order.
linearizability_vs_serializability.ssi: Serializable snapshot isolation is not necessarily linearizable because snapshots intentionally exclude newer writes.

replication_linearizability.single_leader: Potentially linearizable if reads use the true leader or synchronously updated replicas.
replication_linearizability.leaderless: Safest assumption for Dynamo-style replication is not linearizable unless extra mechanisms are added.

strict_quorum_caveat.fact: w+r>n does not by itself guarantee linearizability.
strict_quorum_caveat.reason: During a concurrent write, one reader can see new data and a later reader using a different quorum can still see old data.

cap.better_framing: When partitioned, choose between linearizability and total availability.
cap.scope: Formal CAP considers linearizability and network partitions, not all distributed-system tradeoffs.
cap.chapter_view: Historically influential but limited for practical design.

linearizability_cost.fact: Linearizability is slow even without an actual network partition.
linearizability_cost.reason: Operation latency is tied to uncertainty in network delays.
linearizability_cost.example: Modern multicore memory itself may sacrifice linearizability for performance due to caches/store buffers.

causality.order: Partial order: causally related operations are ordered, concurrent operations are incomparable.
causality.snapshot: A causally consistent snapshot contains causal predecessors of observed effects.

linearizability_vs_causality.causal: Partial order; concurrent branches are allowed.
linearizability_vs_causality.relationship: Linearizability implies causality, but causality does not require linearizability.
linearizability_vs_causality.benefit: Causal consistency can avoid much of linearizability's latency/availability cost.

capturing_causality.requirement: Process causal predecessors before dependent operations.
capturing_causality.metadata: Track versions/data observed by clients; generalized version vectors can capture dependencies.
capturing_causality.cost: Explicitly tracking all dependencies across a database can be expensive.

sequence_number_ordering.single_leader: A replication-log counter creates a causality-consistent total write order.
noncausal_methods: Per-node odd/even or node-ID sequence spaces
sequence_number_ordering.problem: These scalable methods may create unique increasing-looking IDs while violating causal order.

lamport_timestamps.rule: Every node/client carries the maximum counter seen; receiving a greater counter advances the local counter.
lamport_timestamps.guarantee: Compact total ordering consistent with causality.
lamport_timestamps.limitation: Cannot determine whether two operations are concurrent or causally related.
lamport_timestamps.version_vector_difference: Version vectors can distinguish concurrency; Lamport timestamps cannot.

timestamp_order_not_enough.problem: For online uniqueness, a node does not know whether an unseen concurrent operation with a lower timestamp exists.
timestamp_order_not_enough.lesson: A total order is insufficient unless you know the order is finalized.

properties.reliable_delivery: If delivered to one node, eventually delivered to all.
properties.total_order: Every node delivers messages in the same order.

total_order_broadcast.finality: Delivered order cannot be retroactively rearranged.

tob_uses.zookeeper: zxid is an ordered transaction identifier that can act as a fencing token.

cas: Wait for own message to be delivered
linearizable_storage_from_tob.read_problem: Asynchronously materialized replicas can still serve stale reads.
linearizable_read_options: Sequence the read through the log
Get latest log position and wait until caught up

tob_from_linearizable_register.method: Allocate a gap-free sequence number to each message, then deliver consecutively.
tob_from_linearizable_register.equivalence: Total order broadcast, consensus, and sufficiently powerful linearizable registers are reducible to one another.

consensus.informal: Several nodes agree on one irrevocable decision.

flp.result: No deterministic algorithm is guaranteed to reach consensus in the fully asynchronous crash-prone model.
flp.practical_note: Timeouts/failure suspicion or randomness move practical systems outside the theorem's assumptions.

distributed_atomic_commit.single_node: Transaction data is durably written, then a commit record; the durable commit record is the decision point.
distributed_atomic_commit.distributed_problem: Independent commits can succeed on some participants and fail/abort on others.
distributed_atomic_commit.rule: No node may irrevocably commit until all participants can commit.

two_phase_commit.phase2: Commit if all participants vote yes; otherwise abort.

two_pc_promises.participant_yes: Participant has made required data durable, checked constraints/conflicts, and promises it can commit later.
two_pc_promises.coordinator_decision: After all votes, coordinator durably records commit/abort; this is the commit point.
two_pc_promises.retry: After the final decision, coordinator retries final messages until participants learn the outcome.

coordinator_failure.in_doubt: Prepared participant that voted yes but does not know final outcome.
coordinator_failure.cannot_decide: It cannot safely commit or abort by itself.
coordinator_failure.blocking: Must wait for coordinator recovery; thus 2PC is blocking.

three_phase_commit.limitation: Requires bounded timing/perfect failure detection assumptions that do not fit common asynchronous systems.

distributed_transactions.database_internal: Participants run one DB technology and can use optimized internal protocols.
distributed_transactions.heterogeneous: Different databases/message brokers participate through a common protocol.

exactly_once_message_processing.method: Atomically commit message acknowledgement and DB side effects.
exactly_once_message_processing.retry: Abort rolls back both so message can be redelivered safely.
exactly_once_message_processing.boundary: Nontransactional side effects such as email can still duplicate.

xa.name: X/Open eXtended Architecture
xa.purpose: Standard API for 2PC across heterogeneous technologies.
xa.java: Commonly accessed through JTA with JDBC/JMS support.

in_doubt_locks.fact: Prepared transactions retain locks until commit/abort is known.
in_doubt_locks.impact: Coordinator outage or lost logs can block application work for long periods.

heuristic_decisions.definition: Participant unilaterally chooses commit/abort for an in-doubt transaction.

consensus_properties.validity: Decided value was proposed by some node.

fault_tolerant_consensus.progress: Requires a majority to be functioning/reachable.
fault_tolerant_consensus.safety: Safety usually remains intact even if majority loss stops progress.

consensus_as_tob.idea: Repeated consensus decisions determine the next message in a total-order log.

epochs_and_quorums.rule: Leader is unique within an epoch; higher epoch supersedes lower.
epochs_and_quorums.overlap: Quorums must overlap so latest leadership/decision knowledge carries forward.

consensus_vs_2pc.2pc: Coordinator is not elected and every participant must vote yes.
consensus_vs_2pc.consensus: Leader is epoch-based/elected and usually only a majority is needed; recovery after leader change is part of the protocol.

coordination_use_cases.small_ensemble: ZooKeeper commonly uses a small fixed voting group such as 3 or 5 nodes to coordinate many clients.

consensus_equivalent_problems.leader_note: A single leader centralizes these decisions, but fault-tolerant leadership changes still require consensus.

scenario_questions.scenario: Alice sees a new score; Bob later reads an older score.
scenario_questions.question: What was violated?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Linearizability.

scenario_questions.scenario: A read overlaps a write and returns the old value.
scenario_questions.question: Violation?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Not necessarily; concurrent reads may return old or new.

scenario_questions.scenario: One read sees the new value and a later read sees old.
scenario_questions.question: Violation?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Yes; linearizability forbids moving backward.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two nodes both become leader.
scenario_questions.question: What failed?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Linearizable/consensus-backed leader election; split brain occurred.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two users concurrently claim the same username and both succeed.
scenario_questions.question: What guarantee is needed?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Hard uniqueness requires linearizable/consensus-backed decision-making.

scenario_questions.scenario: A queue delivers a resize instruction before storage exposes the uploaded image.
scenario_questions.question: What pattern?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Cross-channel timing dependency.

scenario_questions.scenario: Reader A sees new value from one strict quorum; later B sees old from another.
scenario_questions.question: Why possible?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: w+r>n alone does not ensure linearizability during concurrent propagation.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two datacenters are disconnected but both must accept local writes.
scenario_questions.question: What must be relaxed?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Linearizability if both sides stay available.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two concurrent causal-independent writes occur.
scenario_questions.question: How can causal consistency order them?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Either order; they are incomparable.

scenario_questions.scenario: Node counter=4 receives Lamport max=9.
scenario_questions.question: Next operation?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Advance to 9 then issue counter above 9, typically 10.

scenario_questions.scenario: Node wants to accept username based only on local Lamport order.
scenario_questions.question: Why unsafe?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: An unseen earlier concurrent claim may exist; order is not finalized.

scenario_questions.scenario: Replica has delivered messages 1-4 and receives 6 from gap-free sequence.
scenario_questions.question: What now?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Wait for 5 before delivering 6.

scenario_questions.scenario: Three shards get independent commit requests; one rejects.
scenario_questions.question: What fails?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Atomicity; distributed commit needs coordination.

scenario_questions.scenario: 2PC participant voted yes and coordinator crashes.
scenario_questions.question: Can it abort?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No; it is in doubt and must wait.

scenario_questions.scenario: Coordinator is down 20 minutes after prepare.
scenario_questions.question: Operational effect?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Prepared participants retain locks, blocking other work.

scenario_questions.scenario: Operator forces one in-doubt participant to abort.
scenario_questions.question: What risk?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Heuristic decision may break atomicity.

scenario_questions.scenario: Broker ack and DB write commit together.
scenario_questions.question: Benefit?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Effectively exactly-once processing across those transactional effects.

scenario_questions.scenario: 5-node consensus group loses 2 nodes.
scenario_questions.question: Can it progress?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Yes, 3 remain as a majority.

scenario_questions.scenario: 5-node group loses 3 nodes.
scenario_questions.question: Can it progress?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No majority; progress stops though safety should hold.

scenario_questions.scenario: Term-8 leader returns after term-9 leader was elected.
scenario_questions.question: Who wins?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Term-9 leader.

scenario_questions.scenario: Consensus group repeatedly suspects leader due to flaky link.
scenario_questions.question: What happens?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Leader churn can destroy performance/progress while safety remains.

scenario_questions.scenario: Thousands of workers need partition ownership coordination.
scenario_questions.question: Architecture?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Use a small ZooKeeper/etcd ensemble rather than all workers voting.

scenario_questions.scenario: Service discovery returns slightly stale but usable endpoint.
scenario_questions.question: Does it necessarily need consensus?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No; stale discovery can be acceptable.

short_answer_questions.question: Linearizability vs serializability?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Linearizability is real-time single-object recency; serializability is multi-object transaction isolation in some serial order.

short_answer_questions.question: Why do hard uniqueness constraints need stronger coordination?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Before accepting a claim, the system must know no competing claim can precede it.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the strict quorum trap?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Quorum overlap alone does not ensure that later readers cannot see older values during a concurrent write.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain CAP correctly.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: During a network partition, full linearizability and total availability cannot both be provided on all sides; partition itself is not optional.

short_answer_questions.question: Causal vs linearizable consistency?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Causality orders dependencies and permits concurrency; linearizability totally orders all operations and is stronger.

short_answer_questions.question: How do Lamport timestamps preserve causality?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Max-seen counters are propagated so causal dependencies always increase the timestamp.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can't Lamport timestamps enforce online uniqueness alone?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They provide an order but not finality; unseen earlier operations may still appear.

short_answer_questions.question: What does TOB provide?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Reliable identical message delivery order with final positions.

short_answer_questions.question: How are TOB and consensus related?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Repeated consensus decides successive log entries, and powerful linearizable registers can be transformed into TOB and vice versa.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain FLP accurately.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It rules out guaranteed termination for deterministic consensus in a fully asynchronous crash-prone model, not practical protocols with timeouts/randomness.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is 2PC atomic?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Participants promise commitability before the coordinator records an irrevocable final decision, which is then enforced everywhere.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is 2PC blocking?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: After yes, participants cannot decide alone if the coordinator disappears.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are in-doubt transactions dangerous?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They retain locks and can make large parts of an application unavailable.

short_answer_questions.question: What is XA?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A standardized interface for 2PC across heterogeneous databases/message brokers.

short_answer_questions.question: What are the consensus properties?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Agreement, integrity, validity, termination.

short_answer_questions.question: Safety vs liveness in consensus?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Agreement/integrity/validity are safety; termination is liveness and requires a reachable majority for progress.

short_answer_questions.question: How do epochs/quorums prevent stale leaders?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Higher epochs supersede lower ones and overlapping quorums ensure latest leadership/state knowledge carries into decisions.

short_answer_questions.question: Consensus vs 2PC?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Consensus elects epoch-scoped leaders and normally needs a majority; 2PC has an unelected coordinator and needs every participant.

short_answer_questions.question: Why isn't consensus free?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Voting adds synchronous latency, majority dependence, membership complexity, and leader-election instability under bad networks.

short_answer_questions.question: Why use ZooKeeper/etcd?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They outsource consensus-backed atomic operations, ordering/fencing, failure detection, watches, leader election, and membership.

2PC = prepare promises followed by an irrevocable coordinator decision.
A yes vote surrenders a participant's unilateral right to abort.
2PC is blocking after coordinator failure.
In-doubt participants keep locks.
XA standardizes heterogeneous 2PC but carries major operational costs.
Consensus: agreement, integrity, validity, termination.
First three are safety; termination is liveness.
Consensus needs a majority for progress.
Raft/Paxos/VSR/Zab use epochs and quorums.
Higher epoch supersedes stale leaders.
Election and proposal quorums must overlap.
Consensus normally needs a majority; 2PC needs every participant.
ZooKeeper/etcd outsource consensus-backed coordination.

final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: When a distributed system needs one irrevocable fault-tolerant decision about order, ownership, uniqueness, or commit, the problem tends to reduce to consensus.
